observations.observation: The current verb-forming prefix has a causative reading. Sense 1 separately covers placement into a location or condition. The entry identifies French/Latin ancestry and a spelling relationship with in-. This supports a causative en- constituent; it does not turn negative in- or the suffix -en into this same morpheme.

observations.section: Adjective sense 3; make sure senses 1 and 2
observations.observation: Sure can describe an event certain to occur. The make-sure entry distinguishes bringing about an outcome from checking whether something is true or done. The accepted ensure item selects the former reading. This is a current semantic basis for the free adjective stem, rather than reliance on personal confidence alone.

observations.section: Whole verb, variant and word origin
observations.observation: The selected verb concerns making an event or condition definite; the entry explicitly admits insure especially in North American English. Its origin describes Anglo-Norman/French developments. Modern decomposition is the reviewer's inference from the current prefix, current base and whole meaning, corroborated by the history, rather than a quoted publisher analysis.

observations.section: British sense 1 and American English history
observations.observation: The current outcome meaning matches the accepted ensure projection. The British heading admits the US insure alternative. American historical information connects an en- element and the predecessor of sure. Protection and financial insurance senses are outside the accepted target.

The page describes a productive English causative prefix modeled on French loans and applicable to adjective/noun bases. It separately identifies a Greek location prefix and several suffix functions. Similar letters or broadly causative meanings do not alone justify one canonical identity across these distinct entries.

observations.section: Recipient-information sense, forms and word origin
observations.observation: The current giving-information sense is distinct from informing oneself and influencing something. Listed informed/informing forms preserve inform as a base. The recorded historical shaping formation does not establish a transparent negative-prefix plus document-form lesson for the selected modern meaning.

The adjective can describe possession of knowledge or decisions grounded in understanding. Its plausible derivative relation to inform does not establish that telling a person something suffices for clinical informed consent. Clinical meaning, specialist review and the complete clinical graph remain outside this review.

observations.section: Bring-together and take-away senses; forms; word origin
observations.observation: Gathering from multiple people or places and taking something away are distinguished. Collected and collecting preserve the whole collect base. The historical account connects Latin together/gather material; it is not by itself a present-day teaching graph with col and lect.

observations.section: Gathering, pickup and payment readings; verb word history
observations.observation: The gathering reading is distinguishable from pickup and receiving payment. The historical development includes Latin prefix/root and participial material. A deeper classical analysis would need its own treatment of allomorphs and selected meaning. No such lesson is approved by retaining collect as the intact teaching base.
